name: Diphenhydramine / doxylamine sleep aids

card.summary: Over-the-counter sedating antihistamines used for sleep; guideline bodies rate their insomnia evidence poorly and they carry anticholinergic effects.
card.note: Anticholinergic side effects; AASM guideline recommends against use for insomnia.

quick.overview:
Diphenhydramine and the related doxylamine are first-generation antihistamines that cause drowsiness and are the active ingredients in many nonprescription sleep aids. People turn to them for sleep onset, which looksmaxxers link to skin and facial recovery.

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine's 2017 guideline recommended against diphenhydramine for insomnia, citing poor effectiveness and low-quality evidence.
quick.mechanism: Diphenhydramine is an inverse agonist at histamine H1 receptors and crosses the blood-brain barrier, producing drowsiness. It is also a strong muscarinic antagonist, which explains dry mouth, urinary retention and confusion.
quick.risks: Reported effects include dizziness, dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, and at higher doses confusion, hallucinations and delirium; overdose can cause arrhythmia. Anticholinergic drug use in later life has been linked to cognitive decline, though a 2019 study found no significant association for antihistamines specifically.

lead: Diphenhydramine is a first-generation H1 antihistamine that is a common ingredient in nonprescription sleep aids; the related doxylamine is used similarly [1]. It was discovered in 1943 by George Rieveschl and Fred Huber and was the first FDA-approved prescription antihistamine in the US in 1946 [1].

Guidance on insomnia is cautious: the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommended against its use in 2017 citing low-quality evidence, and a 2022 network meta-analysis in The Lancet found little evidence to guide its use [1].
infobox: OTC in US and Canada, pharmacy medicine in UK [1]

paras: Diphenhydramine acts mainly as an inverse agonist at H1 receptors, and its central effects cause drowsiness. It is also a potent muscarinic antagonist, a sodium channel blocker and a weak serotonin reuptake inhibitor [1].

The most common effects are dizziness and sleepiness. Anticholinergic effects include dry mouth, faster heart rate, urinary retention and constipation; higher doses can cause confusion, hallucinations or delirium, and overdose can cause QT prolongation and arrhythmias [1]. Paradoxical excitation occurs, especially in children [1].

Anticholinergic exposure in later life has been linked to cognitive decline and dementia, but a 2019 JAMA Internal Medicine nested case-control study found the strongest associations for other anticholinergic classes and no significantly increased risk for antihistamines [1].

Evidence assessments for insomnia are summarised in the 2017 American Academy of Sleep Medicine guideline, which recommended against diphenhydramine, and in a 2022 Lancet network meta-analysis that found little evidence to guide its use [1]. No studies found specifically on appearance outcomes.
Diphenhydramine is over-the-counter in the US and Canada, a pharmacy medicine in the UK, and prescription-only in Sweden; it is unscheduled internationally but prohibited in Zambia [1].

timeline.event: Discovered at the University of Cincinnati by George Rieveschl and Fred Huber [1].
First FDA-approved prescription antihistamine in the US [1].
AASM guideline recommends against diphenhydramine for insomnia [1].
JAMA Internal Medicine study finds no significant dementia association for antihistamines [1].
